headline: The AGILE Act of 2019 would have funded and expanded federal support for geothermal energy, but the Senate did not take it up, so it never became law.
what_it_does: If adopted, this bill would have renewed federal funding for geothermal energy research and for a grant program aimed at places with high utility prices through fiscal year 2024. It would have directed the Department of Energy to support drilling-technology work, a heat pump and direct-use program, a prize competition for mineral and geothermal coproduction, and a shared industry drilling database. It would also have required the Department of the Interior to set up a permitting coordination program to speed geothermal reviews on federal land, and would have allowed thermal energy to count toward the federal renewable energy purchase requirement.

who_it_affects.how: They would have gotten federal research funding, a shared drilling data repository, and faster permit reviews for projects on federal land.

who_it_affects.group: Households and businesses in areas with high utility prices
who_it_affects.how: They could have benefited from a federal grant program aimed at geothermal development in those places.

who_it_affects.group: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases
who_it_affects.how: Rules would have applied to geothermal production on federal lands that are already producing oil or gas under an existing lease.

who_it_affects.group: Federal agencies such as the Department of Energy, Interior, and the Bureau of Land Management
who_it_affects.how: They would have been directed to run new research programs, a permitting coordination office, and land-use actions for geothermal energy.
